text: Hi. Hi, everyone. So my name is Phoebe Santos, and I'm going to be talking a bit
today about my master's thesis project, which I did with the Natural History Museum
of London, the Zoological Society of London, and UCL, and we looked
at using large language models for the transcription and information
extraction of ecological data from historical archives.
So to start off with, who can read this?
Or rather, who finds it easy to read?
I certainly find it difficult, and as a researcher trying to sort through hundreds
or thousands of documents like this to explore a single question or find
one piece of information can be extraordinarily time-consuming.
And digitizing and transcribing these records can make them far more searchable
and machine-readable and making them more accessible.
This is the basic premise of our research, looking at how large language models can
be used in an automated way to transcribe handwritten historical records.
So what we wanted to do was build on existing research showing that large language
models can be useful for transcription, but ask whether these approaches can
generalize beyond a single collection.
So a lot of the previous work focuses on developing an approach for a particular
dataset, meaning that the prompts and examples can be tailored to that collection.
We wanted to see whether a single approach could handle different types of
historical records, including differences in handwriting, format, and structure.
Structure became particularly important because we found early on that the models
often struggled to reproduce how information was formatted on the page, and
structure isn't just visual. We, as humans, use it to understand a document.
Paragraphs group ideas, marginal notes add context, and the flow of information on
a page shows how all of the information relates to one another.
So in my thesis, we had two main research questions, the first of which was how
well do our two chosen multimodal LLMs transcribe different types of
historical records?
And the second was whether
prompting strategy as well as
example specificity affect model performance.
And throughout that, looking at whether the models can
preserve the structure within the resulting transcription.
So we had two datasets. One was sourced from the British Library and contained
18th to 19th century handwritten English language records from the
British Colonial Office in India, and the other was from the Natural History Museum
in London and contained handwritten table records relating to their mammal
osteology records.
We used two multimodal LLMs. First was Claude Sonnet 5 with closed weights,
and the second was Qwen 2.5 Vision-Language 32B, which has open weights,
but neither model was altered in any way beyond setting temperature to 0.7.
Both models were given the same user prompt and schema setup, along with
the system prompt and the corresponding document images for transcription.
This is the final zero-shot prompt that we ended up with.
Along with its general transcription task, the model is also told as a
subtask to classify each page into one of three categories based on the
page's structure. We defined those categories and chose them prior.
Those were text, mixed, and table.
And then based off of that classification, the model was given additional
transcription instructions intended to encode the structure within the
resulting transcription.
We then tested zero, one, and few-shot prompting, as well as testing whether giving
the model examples that were dataset specific, so examples that were sourced and
resembled the structure of the dataset that they were transcribing, if that would
have an additional effect on transcription performance.
For our first aim of how well did the models actually transcribe, both models
performed very well overall for records classified as text.
Claude did perform significantly better, but that absolute gap in error difference
was rather small.
However, for the more structured records, such as those in the Natural History
Museum dataset, the difference between the two models was much more pronounced.
So Claude, again, performed significantly better with these more structured
records, while Qwen struggled with creating accurate transcriptions of these
very highly structured records.
For our second aim of how does prompting strategy and example specificity affect
performance, we found that for Claude, again, its performance was very
consistent across all prompting strategies as well as example specificity,
regardless of the dataset and regardless of the structure on the page.
For Qwen, its performance was similarly consistent across prompts for records
classified as text. But on the NHM dataset, where all records were much more
structured, we saw a more distinct effect.
So Qwen's performance improved as it received more examples, and its
performance got an additional boost when those examples were dataset specific.
Overall, this poses LLMs as a viable and accessible tool for transcribing
handwritten historical records, with both tested models performing very well on
unseen, structurally variable data without any prior fine-tuning.
The cost we recorded as well while using Claude, the closed weight model, also
showed LLM-based transcription as a potentially more affordable option for
institutions than existing commercial transcription services.
It's notable, though, that we only included English language records,
and we didn't test any other structures beyond the English convention of writing
from left to right.
Despite these limitations, LLM-based transcription could help bring large
collections of difficult-to-access historical records into use,
while retaining human judgment over what information and structure should be
preserved, and then how those resulting transcriptions should then be used.
